1241.event_title: Ancient Egyptian love songs on lovesickness no physician can cure
1241.event: Love songs from Egypt's Ramesside period, linked with the craftsmen's village of Deir el-Medina, survive on papyri including Papyrus Chester Beatty I, now in Dublin. In one stanza the young man says that his sickness cannot be relieved by the remedies of physicians and that only his beloved's presence can cure him; the songs also describe the beloved herself as a medicine whose sight brings health.
1241.explanation: These are among the oldest surviving love poems in the world, and they already treat love-longing as an illness beyond ordinary medicine.
1241.tie_back: The kural's wife begs her heart to name any medicine at all for a sickness nothing else can cure, and the Egyptian lover, more than three thousand years ago, found that no physician's remedy could touch his.
1241._accuracy_note: A very close parallel, love-sickness that no medicine can cure, though the event is the survival of a poem rather than a datable incident.

1242.event_title: Charlotte Brontë's unanswered letters to Constantin Héger
1242.event: After studying and teaching in Brussels, Charlotte Brontë kept writing to her former teacher Constantin Héger, a married man, making her feelings plain in January 1845. Héger barely replied and by the end of 1845 had stopped replying altogether; in one letter she wrote that a friend had brought her neither letter nor message from him. Four of her letters survive because Héger's wife retrieved the torn letters from the wastebasket and mended them, and his family gave them to the British Library in 1913.
1242.explanation: The letters reveal the private heartbreak behind one of England's greatest novelists and show how long she went on hoping for an answer that never came.
1242.tie_back: The kural's heroine tells her heart that since he has no love for them, its suffering is mere foolishness, and Brontë kept pouring out her feelings to a man who would not reply.
1242._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of grieving over someone who returns no love, though Brontë was not a wife and Héger was never her partner.

1243.event_title: Petrarch first sees Laura in Avignon
1243.event: In 1327, at Avignon, the Italian poet Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch) first saw the woman he called Laura. She became the idealised subject of his chaste love and the main subject of his poetry for the rest of his life, and he gathered his lyrics into the Canzoniere, which eventually held 366 poems.
1243.explanation: Petrarch's lifelong poetry for a love he could never have shaped the European love sonnet for centuries.
1243.tie_back: The kural's heroine asks her heart why it sits thinking and suffering over someone who gives no tender thought in return, and Petrarch spent decades pining in verse for a woman his love could never possess.
1243._accuracy_note: Next-best: a long, one-sided pining matches, but the sources do not record Laura's feelings toward him, and he was a poet, not an abandoned wife.

1244.event_title: Abigail Adams crosses the Atlantic to rejoin John Adams
1244.place: Boston, Massachusetts, to England and Auteuil, France
1244.event: John Adams's long absences on public service, including diplomatic posts in Europe, left his wife Abigail to raise their children and run the farm and household in Massachusetts. In the summer of 1784, after nearly five years apart, she made a month-long voyage from Boston to England with their daughter and joined John in Europe, settling with him at Auteuil, near Paris.
1244.explanation: Her journey ended one of the longest separations of any founding American couple, and her record of the voyage survives in the Adams Papers.
1244.tie_back: The kural's heroine, longing to see her husband, wants her eyes carried to him, and Abigail Adams, after years of longing, went herself to see the husband her heart had followed.
1244._accuracy_note: Next-best: it shows longing to see a distant husband finally acted upon, but not the kural's image of the eyes tormenting the one who stays behind.

1245.event_title: Juliette Drouet's fifty years of devotion to Victor Hugo
1245.event: Juliette Drouet was Victor Hugo's companion for about fifty years and wrote him some 22,000 letters, at least one a day. After the coup of 1851 she helped Hugo escape France with false papers and joined him in Brussels within days of his arrival. Through his long exile she never lived with him, staying with friends, in hotels or in rented rooms, and from 1864 in a house he bought for her, yet she did not leave his side for a single day.
1245.explanation: Her letters are one of the largest records of a single love in literary history.
1245.tie_back: The kural's heroine asks whether she can ever give up a man who does not come to her when she longs for him, and Drouet, never sharing Hugo's home, still could not give him up in fifty years.
1245._accuracy_note: Constancy toward a beloved who kept her at a distance fits, though Hugo did not turn away from her the way the kural's husband seems to.

1246.event_title: Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton remarry in Botswana
1246.place: Kasane, near Chobe Game Park, Botswana
1246.event: Actors Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton married in Montreal in 1964 and divorced in 1974 after stormy years together. About sixteen months later, on 10 October 1975, they secretly remarried in a ceremony performed by a district commissioner at Kasane, near Chobe Game Park in Botswana. The second marriage lasted about nine months.
1246.explanation: Their remarriage became the best-known modern example of a couple whose quarrels could not keep them apart.
1246.tie_back: The kural says the heart cannot even keep up a sulk when it sees the beloved, so its anger is false, and Taylor and Burton's divorce gave way to remarriage as soon as they were together again.
1246._accuracy_note: Shows anger dissolving into reunion, but this was a full divorce rather than a lovers' sulk, and the second marriage soon failed.

1247.event_title: Clara Wieck goes to court against her father to marry Robert Schumann
1247.event: The pianist Clara Wieck and the composer Robert Schumann became secretly engaged in 1837, but her father Friedrich Wieck rejected Robert's written request for her hand and did everything he could to keep them apart. Rather than give Robert up, Clara joined him in taking her father to court for permission to marry; her father disowned her, the court gave them permission in 1840, and they married on 12 September 1840 at Schönefeld near Leipzig.
1247.explanation: For a young woman of her time, suing her own father was a startling break with the duty of obedience expected of a daughter.
1247.tie_back: The kural's heroine says she cannot bear both her desire and her modesty and must give up one, and Clara Wieck, caught between a daughter's duty and her love, finally chose love.
1247._accuracy_note: The conflict between love and social propriety fits, but the restraint was obedience to a father rather than a woman's modesty toward her lover.

1248.event_title: Decembrist wives follow their husbands into Siberian exile
1248.place: From European Russia to Nerchinsk, Siberia
1248.event: After the failed Decembrist revolt of 14 December 1825, its leaders were sent into exile in Siberia. Princess Katherine Trubetskaya left to join her husband about a week behind the prisoner convoy in July 1826, and Princess Maria Volkonskaya, married to Prince Sergei Volkonsky only in January 1825, petitioned Tsar Nicholas I for permission to follow him. To go, Maria had to leave her son with her husband's family and accept that she could never return to European Russia, even if her husband died.
1248.explanation: Their decision became a lasting symbol in Russia of a wife's loyalty at any cost.
1248.tie_back: The kural's heroine chides her heart for running after the one who has gone away, and the Decembrist wives did just that, following their husbands to the far end of the empire.
1248._accuracy_note: Following a departed husband fits well, though these husbands were taken away by force rather than leaving by choice, and the wives' going was admired rather than foolish.

1249.event_title: Rumi's Divan-e Shams after Shams of Tabriz disappears
1249.event: In Konya in the 1240s the scholar and preacher Jalal al-Din Rumi met the wandering dervish Shams al-Din of Tabriz, and the two became close companions who were rarely apart. Shams later disappeared and was never seen again; Rumi turned to poetry, music and dance, and his great collection of lyric poems, the Divan-e Shams, is named after his lost companion and expresses his love and longing for him.
1249.explanation: Rumi's grief for a vanished companion produced some of the most widely read poetry in the world.
1249.tie_back: The kural reminds the heart that the beloved lives within it, so there is no one outside to search for, and Rumi, having lost Shams, came to speak in his name in poems that carried Shams within them.
1249._accuracy_note: The beloved living on inside the one who lost him fits well, though the bond was spiritual friendship rather than marriage.

1250.event_title: Queen Victoria's long seclusion after Prince Albert's death
1250.event: Prince Albert died of typhoid fever in 1861 at the age of 42, and Queen Victoria sank into deep mourning. She wore black for the rest of her life and for years rarely appeared in public, spending more than a decade largely in seclusion. She was widely criticised for her withdrawal, her popularity sank, and a strong republican movement developed in Britain.
1250.explanation: Her case shows how holding on to grief for a lost husband cost even a queen her standing with her people.
1250.tie_back: The kural warns that keeping in the heart the one who has gone will cost still more of one's beauty and standing, and Victoria's devotion to the absent Albert cost her much of her public esteem.
1250._accuracy_note: The cost of clinging to an absent partner fits well, though Albert's absence was death rather than desertion.
